subject: music
title: Krautrock: West Germany's new music, 1968 to 1977
dek: Around 1968 a generation of young West German musicians decided they did not want to copy British and American rock or play their parents' Schlager. In communes, castles and home studios they built a new kind of music out of repetition, electronics and tape editing, and that music went on to shape post-punk, ambient, techno and hip-hop.
era: c. 1968 to 1977, with long effects to the present
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in Wikipedia's articles on krautrock, Can, Kraftwerk, Neu!, Faust, Harmonia, Cluster, Conny Plank, Damo Suzuki, the Zodiak Free Arts Lab, Tangerine Dream's Phaedra and Kraftwerk's Autobahn, and in the books those articles cite. Chart positions are given only where I could check them. The lesson does not quote musicians directly except for one well-documented line from Faust, and it has no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

timeline.label: Tangerine Dream is founded in West Berlin
timeline.detail: Edgar Froese starts the group that will become the best-known name in electronic 'cosmic' music.

timeline.label: Can forms in Cologne; the Zodiak Free Arts Lab opens in Berlin
timeline.detail: Holger Czukay, Irmin Schmidt, Jaki Liebezeit and Michael Karoli form the Inner Space, soon renamed Can. In spring, Conrad Schnitzler, Hans-Joachim Roedelius and Boris Schaak open the Zodiak, a club in Kreuzberg where anyone could improvise on the instruments left in its rooms.

timeline.label: First records; the Zodiak closes
timeline.detail: Amon Düül II releases Phallus Dei and Can releases Monster Movie. The Zodiak closes in early 1969 after only a few months.

timeline.label: Kraftwerk begins; Damo Suzuki joins Can
timeline.detail: Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider leave the group Organisation and start Kraftwerk in Düsseldorf. In late May, Czukay and Liebezeit hear Damo Suzuki busking in Munich and invite him to sing with Can that night. Tangerine Dream releases Electronic Meditation.

timeline.label: Neu! and Faust; Tago Mago
timeline.detail: Klaus Dinger and Michael Rother leave Kraftwerk and form Neu!. Faust releases its first album on clear vinyl. Can releases the double album Tago Mago, and its single 'Spoon' reaches the German singles chart.

timeline.label: Neu! and Ege Bamyasi
timeline.detail: Neu!'s first album, produced with Conny Plank, introduces the steady beat later called motorik. Can releases Ege Bamyasi.

timeline.label: Virgin brings German bands to Britain
timeline.detail: Virgin Records releases The Faust Tapes for 49 pence, the price of a single. Faust records Faust IV, which includes a twelve-minute track called 'Krautrock'. Can releases Future Days.

timeline.label: Autobahn, Phaedra and Harmonia
timeline.detail: Kraftwerk's Autobahn has a 22-minute title track; the album later reaches number 5 on Billboard's US album chart in May 1975. Tangerine Dream's Phaedra reaches number 15 in the UK. Harmonia, a trio of Cluster and Michael Rother living in Forst, releases Musik von Harmonia.

timeline.label: Brian Eno visits Harmonia
timeline.detail: Eno records with Harmonia in Forst. The sessions are released much later, in 1997, as Tracks and Traces. Harmonia breaks up the same year.

timeline.label: Trans-Europe Express and Bowie's Low
timeline.detail: Kraftwerk releases Trans-Europe Express. David Bowie, living in West Berlin, releases Low and "Heroes", the first two albums of his Berlin trilogy with Eno.

timeline.label: Kraftwerk reaches the Bronx
timeline.detail: Afrika Bambaataa and the Soul Sonic Force release 'Planet Rock', built on the melody of Kraftwerk's 'Trans-Europe Express' and the rhythm of 'Numbers'.

timeline.label: Krautrocksampler
timeline.detail: Julian Cope's book Krautrocksampler starts a revival of interest in the music among British and American listeners.

fun_fact.title: A singer found on the street
fun_fact.text: Can's best-known singer joined the band in a single evening. In late May 1970, Holger Czukay and Jaki Liebezeit saw a young Japanese traveller, Damo Suzuki, busking outside the Blow Up club in Munich and asked him to perform with Can that same night. He stayed for three years and sang on Tago Mago, Ege Bamyasi and Future Days.

sections.title: Before krautrock: American radio, Schlager and a silent past

blocks.text: West German teenagers in the 1950s and 1960s grew up with two kinds of popular music. The first was Schlager: sentimental, carefully produced German songs about love, holidays and home, played on television and family radio. The second was British and American rock and roll, heard on the radio stations of the occupying armies and in clubs such as the Star-Club in Hamburg, where the Beatles had played before they were famous. Many German bands of the early 1960s simply copied English-language beat music.

For a young person in 1968, both options felt borrowed. Schlager belonged to the parents' generation, the same generation that had lived through the Nazi era and rarely talked about it. Anglo-American rock belonged to the countries whose armies were still stationed in West Germany. The student movement of 1968 was asking hard questions about the Nazi past, about the Vietnam War and about American power. Some young musicians started asking a similar question about sound: what would a German popular music look like if it did not come from either of these places?

This is the background that writers on the period stress again and again. The musicians who became known as krautrock bands were trying to escape both American influence and conservative German entertainment, and to build a new popular culture from close to nothing. They took ideas from free jazz, from avant-garde composers such as Karlheinz Stockhausen, from psychedelic rock and from the Velvet Underground, but they tried to put them together in a way nobody had heard before.
Krautrock is not one style. Can, Kraftwerk, Faust and Tangerine Dream sound very different from each other. What they share is a set of habits:

items: Repetition. Many tracks are built on a single groove that repeats for ten or twenty minutes, changing slowly instead of moving through verses and choruses.

The motorik beat. A steady, driving drum pattern with a heavy kick drum that seems to push the music forward like a car on a motorway. Klaus Dinger of Neu! and Jaki Liebezeit of Can are the drummers most associated with it.
Electronics. Synthesizers, organs, tape machines and home-made devices, especially in Kraftwerk, Tangerine Dream, Cluster and Klaus Schulze.
Long improvisation, followed by editing. Bands often recorded hours of jamming and then cut it into finished pieces on tape.
The studio as an instrument. The producer and engineer were part of the band's sound, not just technicians.

blocks.text: The music played in Germany was often called kosmische Musik, meaning 'cosmic music', especially for the electronic groups. The word 'krautrock' came from Britain. 'Kraut' was an old British slang word for Germans, and the term seems to have started as a joke in the early 1970s, either from the DJ John Peel or from the paper Melody Maker, where these bands found their first enthusiastic foreign audience. Faust even called a 1973 track 'Krautrock', and later said that when the English started talking about krautrock, they thought the English were 'taking the piss'. The writer Julian Cope argued that krautrock is really a British idea: a name for how British listeners heard this music, not a name the German scene used for itself.

sections.title: Berlin: the Zodiak and the cosmic musicians

blocks.text: In spring 1968, the artists Conrad Schnitzler and Hans-Joachim Roedelius, with Boris Schaak, opened the Zodiak Free Arts Lab in a back room of a theatre building on the Landwehr Canal in Kreuzberg, West Berlin. It could only open late at night, after the theatre's performances had ended. One room was painted all white and the other all black, and both were filled with instruments and amplifiers that anyone could use. Conventional songs were looked down on; a phrase from the time was that songs were 'bourgeois'.

Tangerine Dream, founded by Edgar Froese in 1967, played there often, sometimes for five or six hours a night. Klaus Schulze and the musicians who later formed Ash Ra Tempel also passed through. The club closed in early 1969, but its people kept working together. Schnitzler and Schulze played on Tangerine Dream's first album, Electronic Meditation (1970). Schnitzler, Roedelius and Dieter Moebius then formed Kluster, later renamed Cluster.

Tangerine Dream moved steadily toward electronic music built on sequencers, which repeat a pattern of notes automatically. Their album Phaedra (1974), released in Britain by Virgin, reached number 15 on the UK albums chart with almost no radio play, carried by word of mouth. In Munich, the Amon Düül commune produced Amon Düül II, whose Phallus Dei (1969) mixed psychedelic rock with long, tribal-sounding jams, and Florian Fricke's Popol Vuh began writing the music for Werner Herzog's films, starting with Aguirre, the Wrath of God (1972).

sections.title: Can: composers who wanted to play rock

blocks.text: Can was formed in Cologne in 1968, first under the name the Inner Space. Two of its members, the bassist Holger Czukay and the keyboard player Irmin Schmidt, had studied with Karlheinz Stockhausen, the leading avant-garde composer in West Germany. The drummer Jaki Liebezeit came from free jazz, and the guitarist Michael Karoli was younger and loved rock. The combination mattered: Can had the training of classical composers but wanted the physical energy of a rock band.

Their first singer was Malcolm Mooney, an American sculptor living in Europe, who sang on Monster Movie (1969). After Mooney left the band in 1970, Czukay and Liebezeit found Damo Suzuki, a young traveller from Kobe, busking in Munich and invited him on stage that same night. Suzuki often sang in a mix of English, Japanese and invented sounds, using his voice as another instrument. With him Can made the three albums most people now consider their best: Tago Mago (1971), Ege Bamyasi (1972) and Future Days (1973).

Can set up their own studio, also called Inner Space, in Schloss Nörvenich, a castle near Cologne. They would improvise for hours with the tape running, and Czukay would then edit the best passages together with a razor blade, building finished tracks from many pieces of a jam. Liebezeit's drumming, extremely tight and repetitive but never mechanical, became the band's foundation. Can also had real hits in Germany: 'Spoon' (1971) and 'I Want More' (1976) both reached national singles charts.

Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider first played together in a quintet called Organisation, which released one album, Tone Float, in 1970 and then split. The two then started Kraftwerk, meaning 'power station', and set up their own studio in Düsseldorf, which they named Kling Klang. Their early records were made with the producer Conny Plank and sound much closer to the rest of the krautrock scene: flute, organ, feedback and long jams.

For a short time Kraftwerk included the drummer Klaus Dinger and the guitarist Michael Rother. In 1971 the two left and formed Neu!, which means 'New!'. Neu!'s first album (1972), produced by Plank, is built on the motorik beat: Dinger plays a steady, almost unchanging pulse while Rother's guitar floats over it. Neu! released three albums, Neu! (1972), Neu! 2 (1973) and Neu! '75 (1975). They sold little at the time, but later musicians, from David Bowie to Stereolab and Radiohead, named them as an influence.

Kraftwerk, meanwhile, moved toward machines. Autobahn (1974) opens with a 22-minute track that imitates a drive on the motorway, with synthesizers standing in for engines and horns and a simple, cheerful vocal. The album reached number 5 on Billboard's US album chart in May 1975, an extraordinary result for an experimental German record. Radio-Activity (1975), Trans-Europe Express (1977) and The Man-Machine (1978) followed. By then Kraftwerk had become something new: a band that presented itself as almost robotic, writing short electronic pop songs about trains, radio and computers.

sections.title: Faust, Harmonia and the studio wizards

blocks.text: Faust was put together around 1970 by Uwe Nettelbeck, a former music journalist, and the band secured a recording contract with Polydor. The band lived and recorded in a converted schoolhouse in the village of Wümme. Their first album came out on clear vinyl in a clear sleeve printed with an X-ray of a human fist. It sold very poorly. In 1973 Virgin Records released The Faust Tapes, a collage of studio fragments, for 49 pence, the price of a single. It sold an estimated 60,000 to 100,000 copies in Britain and introduced many British teenagers to German experimental music, including the young Julian Cope.

Harmonia was a smaller, quieter story. In 1973 Moebius and Roedelius of Cluster joined Michael Rother of Neu! in the rural village of Forst, where they lived and recorded together. Musik von Harmonia (1974) and Deluxe (1975) sold little. In 1976 Brian Eno, already a fan, came to Forst to record with them. Those sessions stayed on the shelf until 1997, when they were released as Tracks and Traces.

Behind many of these records stood Conny Plank, a producer and engineer whose studio near Cologne became a meeting place for the scene. Plank worked on early Kraftwerk records, on Neu!, Cluster and Harmonia, and later on records by British and international bands. Plank and Czukay showed that the person at the mixing desk could be as creative as the person holding the guitar.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere at the same time

blocks.text: In Britain, the same years saw the rise of progressive rock: Pink Floyd, King Crimson, Soft Machine and Yes. Prog shared krautrock's long tracks and interest in electronics, but most prog bands leaned on virtuoso solos and on classical music. Krautrock bands more often aimed for trance through repetition. British labels such as Virgin, which signed Tangerine Dream and Faust, became the main bridge between the two scenes.

In France, the drummer Christian Vander founded Magma in 1969 and sang in an invented language, Kobaïan, another example of a European band refusing to sound American. In Jamaica, King Tubby and Lee 'Scratch' Perry were turning the recording studio into an instrument at almost exactly the same moment as Czukay and Plank, stripping reggae tracks down to drum, bass and echo to create dub.

In Japan, Isao Tomita's synthesizer album Snowflakes Are Dancing (1974) brought electronic music to a wide audience, and in 1978 Haruomi Hosono, Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi formed Yellow Magic Orchestra, which openly built on Kraftwerk's example of a band made of machines. On the other side of the Berlin Wall, rock in East Germany needed a state performance licence. The Puhdys, who received theirs in 1969, became the most famous band of the official East German rock scene, working inside limits that West German musicians did not face.

By the late 1970s the original krautrock era was over. Neu! and Harmonia had broken up, Can's classic lineup had changed, and Kraftwerk had moved into electronic pop. But the music's influence was just starting.

David Bowie moved to West Berlin in 1976 and, with Brian Eno and the producer Tony Visconti, made Low (1977), "Heroes" (1977) and Lodger (1979). The instrumental 'V-2 Schneider' on "Heroes" is named after Florian Schneider. The post-punk bands covered in the post-punk lesson, including Public Image Ltd, Joy Division, Wire, Gang of Four and the Fall, drew on krautrock's repetition and coldness; the Fall even recorded a song called 'I Am Damo Suzuki' (1985).

Kraftwerk's influence on Black American dance music was just as large. 'Planet Rock' (1982) by Afrika Bambaataa and the Soul Sonic Force, discussed in the hip-hop origins lesson, borrowed from 'Trans-Europe Express' and 'Numbers', and the Detroit techno producers discussed in the Chicago house lesson treated Kraftwerk as founders of their sound. Later bands such as Stereolab, Sonic Youth, Radiohead and LCD Soundsystem have all pointed back to Neu! and Can, and Julian Cope's 1995 book Krautrocksampler helped a new generation find the records.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: The krautrock musicians tried to build a popular music that owed nothing to their parents or to America. Is it possible to create a truly new sound by rejecting what came before, or did they succeed mainly by combining borrowed pieces in a new way?
